title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text: The fact that I studied R led me to question how classroom programming stacks up against the technologies referred to in job advertisements. For a person looking into technology careers, would learning Python, web development, or cloud infrastructure be a useful next move? I collected two of the Hacker News “Who is hiring?” threads and then compared them using a fixed list of 20 technology categories. Python is mentioned in 27.7% of the hiring comments that remained from September 2026, which is the highest proportion among the categories in question, while I was surprised to find out that R appears in 0 of 256 postings. Python is a reasonable place to start for this kind of job. However, the analysis does not indicate which skill will yield the highest payoff or increase an individual’s chances of getting an offer.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text:
Where the data comes from
The data comes from the September 2025 and September 2026 threads. The acquisition metadata were saved on 19 September 2026. I used an R scraper with rvest to collect public HTML, cache the pages, and wait 30 seconds between each new page request. The current robots.txt asks for this delay and allows access to /item. The workflow does not get around logins, paywalls, or CAPTCHAs. While Hacker News has an official API, I used HTML extraction to practice the rvest workflow required for this assignment. No new requests are needed to reproduce the saved analysis.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text:
Turning comments into measurements
The files contain 863 comments, some of which are replies. I kept the top-level comments that include text, removed duplicate comment IDs, and excluded 10 entries identified during review as discussions, personal job-seeking or service offers, or insufficiently informative content. The final dataset consists of 294 hiring comments from 2025 and 256 from 2026. The IDs of the excluded entries together with the reasons for their exclusion are saved with the code. Each comment is counted only once even if it promotes more than one job; likewise, the same employer can be listed more than once.
Keyword matching also has to be checked. I only caught the “Go” bug because its count jumped from 26 to 42 between two runs on identical data, triggered by phrases like “Go for it” and “Go-To-Market”. Updating the matching rules resolved those false positives and captured the all-caps GO spelling. For the other options, the criteria are intentionally kept narrow: SQL counts the single term, while Postgres includes PostgreSQL. It is not appropriate to add the percentages since comments can refer to both. These adjustments cover mentions such as company technology stacks, not the verified requirements for each advertised role.


Show code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "skill_share_2026.png"))








Figure 1: Leading technology categories in retained September 2026 hiring comments. Ties at rank 12 are included.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
section: What was the difference between the two snapshots?
text:
What was the difference between the two snapshots?
TypeScript and React make up 20.3% and 19.9% of the retained comments from 2026, respectively. Their proportions are 8.3 and 8.0 percentage points lower than in the 2025 snapshot. These are the observed differences, not an indication of a widespread decline in demand for web development.
Comparing two September threads eliminates one aspect of the seasonal mismatch by using the same calendar month, but it does not keep the hiring population constant. The September 2026 data was still incomplete at the time of collection, and each thread includes different employers and positions. Because this is a self-selecting online community, not a random selection of jobs, keyword rules may also miss abbreviations or count occasional references. For these reasons I give the comparison only a descriptive account rather than treating these differences as evidence about the wider labour market.


Show code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "skill_change.png"))








Figure 2: Observed differences in mention shares across the two saved September threads. These are descriptive comparisons, not causal effects or population estimates.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
section: What is the right thing for a student to do in this situation?
text:
What is the right thing for a student to do in this situation?
If a student is already using R and wants to learn about the types of jobs listed here, I suggest they create a small Python project by obtaining data, cleaning it, and publishing a reproducible analysis. While Python is prominent, such a project should be seen as a reasonable experiment rather than a sure way to secure a job. Alternatively, a student aiming for a career in web development could build a TypeScript/React application, since both are still frequently mentioned even though they have lower proportions in this comparison.
Before you decide on a longer course, look at a selection of advertisements that correspond to your location, level of experience, and the position you want. Determine which technologies are essential and which only refer to the employer’s technology stack. This matters because the dataset includes senior engineering positions, junior ones, and non-technical roles. The lack of a verified R keyword match in this case does not prove that R is unimportant for jobs in economics or statistics.

            `2025 count` = n_2025,
            `2025 (%)` = round(100 * share_2025, 1),
            `2026 count` = n_2026,
            `2026 (%)` = round(100 * share_2026, 1),
            `Change (pp)` = round(change_pp, 1)) |>

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text:
Takeaway
Python is a practical first language for students exploring this hiring community. Use the ranking to select the ads and skills to review, then check the actual positions. Although two scraped threads can help you make a well-focused decision, they cannot show what all employers want.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text: A study looks at a new treatment and reports \(p=0.03\). Within hours, a press release declares the finding “97% likely to be real,” and readers naturally infer there is only a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true. This seems intuitive, simple, and satisfying. It is in fact entirely incorrect. A p-value does not measure the probability that a hypothesis is correct, nor does it quantify the likelihood that your finding was a fluke. Confusing what the data tells us about a hypothesis and what a hypothesis tells us about the data is the most common misunderstanding in applied statistics—and overcoming this mistake involves recognizing a subtle mental trick.

title: What a p-value actually tells you

Within hours, a press release declares the finding “97% likely to be real,” and readers naturally infer there is only a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true. This seems intuitive, simple, and satisfying. It is in fact entirely incorrect. A p-value does not measure the probability that a hypothesis is correct, nor does it quantify the likelihood that your finding was a fluke. Confusing what the data tells us about a hypothesis and what a hypothesis tells us about the data is the most common misunderstanding in applied statistics—and overcoming this mistake involves recognizing a subtle mental trick.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
section: Why the Brain Flips the Conditional
text:
Why the Brain Flips the Conditional
The reason the error remains is due to an unconscious substitution. When researchers carry out experiments in order to find out about reality, they ask themselves: How likely is my hypothesis given these results? However, standard significance testing is unable to provide an answer to that question; it only answers a reversed one: Assuming that the null hypothesis is true, how likely is the data in question? Since people never naturally look for the probability of their data in a hypothetical situation in which nothing at all works, the brain automatically replaces the question that was originally wanted with the one that has actually been calculated.
It is straightforward to identify the flaw when looking at ordinary language: although it is clearly true that most professional basketball players are tall, it is absurd to say that most tall people are professional basketball players. The two statements involve the same categories, yet reversing the conditional completely changes the truth of the claim. Similarly, when we switch the categories from ‘basketball players’ to ‘data’ and ‘hypotheses’, our instinct fails to recognise that the same reversal is taking place.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
What the Math Actually Says
A p-value is formally defined as: \[p = P(T \geq t_{\text{obs}} \mid H_0 \text{ true})\] What people mistakenly hear is the inverted posterior probability: \[P(H_0 \text{ true} \mid \text{data})\] These are fundamentally different quantities. The second equation cannot even be computed from the p-value alone; moving from \(P(\text{data} \mid H_0)\) to \(P(H_0 \mid \text{data})\) requires Bayes’ rule, which demands an explicit prior belief about the plausibility of \(H_0\) before the experiment began.
The p-value contains zero information about priors. Instead, it operates strictly inside a hypothetical baseline:

Assume the null hypothesis is completely true.
Generate the sampling distribution of your test statistic under that assumption.
Measure the probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as \(t_{\text{obs}}\)

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Visualizing the Null Distribution
The cleanest way to see this distinction is to simulate the null distribution directly in R: For simplicity the simulation below treats the test as one-sided, counting only results at least as large as the observed statistic.

set.seed(42)

n          <- 30
obs_stat   <- 0.34
null_stats <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)))

p_value <- mean(null_stats >= obs_stat)

h <- hist(null_stats, breaks = 50, plot = FALSE)

plot(h, col = "gray90", border = "gray70",
     main = "Simulated Null Distribution",
     xlab = "Sample mean under H0",
     xlim = c(-0.8, 0.8))

tail_bins <- which(h$mids >= obs_stat)
rect(h$breaks[tail_bins], 0,
     h$breaks[tail_bins + 1], h$counts[tail_bins],
     col = "tomato", border = "gray70")

abline(v = obs_stat, col = "red3", lwd = 2, lty = 2)







Figure 1: 10,000 simulated experiments in a world where the null hypothesis is true. The shaded tail is the p-value.





A \(p\)-value of 2.9% means that t if the effect were exactly zero, roughly 3 in every 100 studies like yours would produce data this extreme or more so. It says nothing about whether the effect is zero.
The histogram visualizes 10,000 experiments conducted in a world where \(H_0\) is true. The red shaded tail represents the proportion of simulated trials that produced a statistic at or beyond our observed value \(t_{\text{obs}}\). The area of that tail is the p-value: a tail probability under an assumed null model, not the probability that the null model itself is correct.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
A Brief Historical Accident
When Ronald Fisher introduced the 0.05 threshold in his 1925 classic Statistical Methods for Research Workers, he intended it as an informal, practical benchmark for identifying anomalies worthy of a second look—partly to save researchers from having to interpolate across extensive printed tables. He never conceived it as an absolute dividing line between truth and falsehood, nor as a posterior measure of scientific certainty.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Takeaway
A p-value tells you how surprising your data would be if nothing were happening; it never tells you the probability that nothing is happening.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
References
Fisher, R. A. (1925). Statistical Methods for Research Workers. Oliver and Boyd.
